frictionVectors.title: European Gas Diversification
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong control over its gas sector, but European efforts to diversify supply reduce its long-term pricing leverage. Sonatrach still anchors export strategy and foreign investment terms.

frictionVectors.title: Morocco-Sahel Security Arc
frictionVectors.details: Rivalry with Morocco and instability across the Sahel complicate border security, pipeline planning, and regional diplomatic influence. External powers increasingly compete for access and partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: Lobito Corridor Contest
frictionVectors.details: The corridor has become a strategic platform for US, European, and Chinese competition over critical-mineral supply chains. Angola gains infrastructure leverage but risks serving as an export conduit with limited domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese Debt and Oil Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Debt-linked infrastructure and continued dependence on hydrocarbons constrain policy autonomy. Efforts to diversify production have not yet displaced foreign-financed extraction as the core economic model.

frictionVectors.title: Niger Trade and Pipeline Dispute
frictionVectors.details: Strained relations with Niger threaten transit flows and complicate the operation of the Niger-Benin oil export corridor. Benin's port and customs leverage are increasingly entangled with regional political disputes.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Militant Spillover
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent activity near the northern borders places pressure on roads, agricultural zones, and emerging industrial infrastructure. Security cooperation with regional and external partners is expanding but remains costly and uneven.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers Partnership Tension
frictionVectors.details: Botswana is pressing for greater domestic value capture and stronger marketing terms as the diamond market weakens. The partnership remains valuable, but negotiations expose the limits of dependence on a foreign-linked operator.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral Diversification Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Competition for copper, nickel, lithium, and other minerals is drawing interest from global investors and strategic powers. Botswana must balance rapid infrastructure development with regulatory control and local processing.

frictionVectors.title: Gold Control and Smuggling
frictionVectors.details: The junta is seeking tighter state control over industrial and artisanal gold, but insecurity and informal networks continue to divert production. Foreign operators and regional intermediaries remain central to supply-chain access.

frictionVectors.title: Security Dependence on Russia
frictionVectors.details: Expanded cooperation with Russian security actors reduces reliance on Western partners but creates new external dependence and accountability risks. Persistent militant violence continues to undermine effective sovereign control over mining zones and transport corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Opaque mineral contracts
frictionVectors.details: Gold and rare-mineral activity remains difficult for the state to regulate, with informal production and external trading networks limiting public revenue capture.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda border tensions
frictionVectors.details: Mutual accusations over armed groups and cross-border insecurity continue to divert resources toward defense and complicate regional economic integration.

frictionVectors.title: External dependence in strategic infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Ports, airports, tourism and digital connectivity rely heavily on foreign capital and development finance, creating exposure to competing European, Chinese and transatlantic interests.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime security burden
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde must balance sovereignty over its maritime zone with reliance on foreign patrol, intelligence and enforcement support against trafficking.

frictionVectors.title: Oil, gas and mining leverage
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon and mining projects depend on foreign firms and lenders, while weak transparency limits the state's ability to convert resource activity into broad domestic gains.

frictionVectors.title: Transport corridor insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the Northwest and Southwest, alongside instability near the Far North, threatens roads, agricultural supply chains and regional transit routes.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security and mining nexus
frictionVectors.details: Russian-linked security forces retain influence around regime protection and mining activity, raising concerns that security assistance is exchanged for privileged access to gold and other resources.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese infrastructure-for-resources exposure
frictionVectors.details: Road, mining and commercial projects involving Chinese entities offer needed infrastructure but risk reinforcing opaque concessions and weak domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: State finances and political stability remain tightly linked to oil exports, pipeline access and foreign operating partners, leaving sovereignty vulnerable to price and contract shocks.

frictionVectors.title: Security-partner transition
frictionVectors.details: The recalibration of ties with France and other Western partners creates openings for Russia, Gulf states and regional actors while increasing uncertainty around counterterrorism support and border control.

frictionVectors.title: Mayotte and maritime sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: The unresolved dispute with France over Mayotte limits diplomatic room and fuels domestic political pressure. French control of the island also shapes access to surrounding maritime resources and security arrangements.

frictionVectors.title: Aid and connectivity dependence
frictionVectors.details: Comoros remains reliant on external donors, remittances, and foreign-backed transport and energy projects, reducing its leverage over strategic infrastructure.

highlights: Critical minerals draw competing foreign interests

frictionVectors.title: Minerals and contract sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Cobalt, copper, lithium, and gold attract Chinese, Western, and regional actors, while weak oversight leaves the state struggling to capture full value from strategic resources.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern security and regional interference
frictionVectors.details: Armed groups and cross-border tensions involving Rwanda and other neighboring states continue to obstruct Kinshasa's control over territory, mines, and transport corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-operated oil production remains the core source of export earnings and fiscal capacity, leaving the country exposed to price cycles and limited domestic value addition.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure-for-resources exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese financing and construction have expanded roads and public works but also increase dependence on external contractors, creditors, and opaque commercial terms.

highlights: Cocoa value capture is gradually improving

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa sovereignty and foreign processing
frictionVectors.details: Côte d'Ivoire is strengthening domestic processing and producer regulation, but global traders and volatile prices still capture substantial value from its cocoa economy.

frictionVectors.title: Port and security competition
frictionVectors.details: Abidjan's port expansion increases strategic importance while Gulf, European, Chinese, and regional actors compete for logistics influence. Spillover insecurity from the Sahel remains a persistent infrastructure and investment risk.

frictionVectors.title: Base politics and sovereign autonomy
frictionVectors.details: U.S., Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military presences generate rent and security guarantees but constrain Djibouti's strategic freedom and create exposure to great-power rivalry.

frictionVectors.title: Port corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: The economy depends heavily on maritime facilities and trade with landlocked Ethiopia, leaving revenue and infrastructure security vulnerable to regional conflict, debt pressures, and external operators.

frictionVectors.title: GERD and Nile security
frictionVectors.details: Egypt continues to oppose binding Ethiopian rules for filling and operating the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam. The dispute remains tied to national water security and broader Red Sea competition.

frictionVectors.title: External financing and asset sales
frictionVectors.details: IMF-backed reforms and Gulf investment provide liquidity but increase foreign influence over strategic assets, including ports, property, and state-linked enterprises.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon decline and foreign operators
frictionVectors.details: Falling crude output is narrowing fiscal space and increasing reliance on foreign technical partners and investment to sustain offshore production and LNG infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Gulf of Guinea maritime security
frictionVectors.details: Offshore energy assets remain exposed to piracy, illegal fishing, and regional insecurity, encouraging dependence on external naval and security cooperation.

frictionVectors.title: Ethiopian sea-access pressure
frictionVectors.details: Ethiopia's search for reliable maritime access keeps Eritrean ports and border areas strategically sensitive. Any renewed confrontation could rapidly internationalize the Red Sea security environment.

frictionVectors.title: Mining dependence and sanctions exposure
frictionVectors.details: Mining revenues and foreign technical partnerships remain important but narrow the country's economic options, while diplomatic isolation limits bargaining flexibility.

frictionVectors.title: Economic reliance on South Africa
frictionVectors.details: Trade, remittances, transport links, and access to regional infrastructure leave Eswatini highly exposed to South African economic and political conditions.

frictionVectors.title: Diplomatic competition over Taiwan
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini's formal relationship with Taiwan attracts diplomatic and development support but also exposes the kingdom to sustained pressure from China and limits some financing options.

frictionVectors.title: Nile dam confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam expands Ethiopia's control over electricity generation but remains a major source of tension with Egypt and Sudan over downstream water security.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea access and infrastructure finance
frictionVectors.details: Ethiopia's pursuit of dependable port access is entangled with regional rivalry and external security actors. Debt restructuring and reliance on foreign infrastructure capital further constrain strategic freedom.

highlights: Junta tightens control over oil and manganese
France remains influential but less dominant

frictionVectors.title: Mining contract renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The transitional government is seeking greater state participation and domestic processing in manganese and other minerals. Investors may resist terms that raise fiscal and local-content obligations.

frictionVectors.title: Port and logistics dependence
frictionVectors.details: Libreville and mineral-export corridors remain exposed to foreign operators, financing, and technical capacity. Efforts to diversify partners could generate friction with established French and Asian commercial interests.

highlights: Senegal remains the decisive external partner
Ports and fisheries shape strategic autonomy

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries enforcement gap
frictionVectors.details: Limited maritime surveillance leaves Gambian waters vulnerable to foreign overfishing and opaque licensing arrangements. This constrains local food security and weakens state capture of fisheries revenue.

frictionVectors.title: Transport corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: Trade relies heavily on Senegalese road, transit, and regional logistics networks. Political or administrative friction with Dakar could quickly affect fuel supplies, food imports, and access to the port of Banjul.

highlights: Gold sector remains central to sovereignty

frictionVectors.title: Illegal mining and water security
frictionVectors.details: Unregulated gold mining, including activity involving foreign-linked operators, continues to damage farmland and water systems. Enforcement is politically difficult because the sector provides livelihoods and informal financing.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Ghana is seeking more local value addition in gold, bauxite, and emerging lithium production while managing investor and creditor demands. Fiscal constraints reduce its leverage over foreign capital and infrastructure providers.

highlights: Bauxite and Simandou reshape national leverage
Junta centralizes control over mining deals

frictionVectors.title: Simandou infrastructure contest
frictionVectors.details: Rail, port, and mining development at Simandou could transform Guinea's export capacity but increases dependence on large foreign consortia and external financing. The government must balance state participation with demands for rapid project execution.

frictionVectors.title: Bauxite enclave risk
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms dominate much of the bauxite value chain, while local processing remains limited. Contract reviews and local-content requirements may improve state capture but risk delaying investment and provoking arbitration.

highlights: Cashew exports remain the economic anchor
Weak institutions limit control of coastal resources

frictionVectors.title: Cashew trade dependence
frictionVectors.details: Exporters and foreign buyers capture substantial influence over the cashew economy, while the state has limited capacity to regulate pricing, storage, and processing. Seasonal market disruptions can quickly create fiscal and social stress.

frictionVectors.title: Port and maritime vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Bissau's port, fisheries, and coastal waters remain vulnerable to opaque concessions, foreign commercial pressure, and illicit trafficking. Weak oversight makes resource revenues difficult to secure and infrastructure planning highly dependent on external partners.

highlights: Ports and energy remain strategic pressure points

frictionVectors.title: External debt and infrastructure leverage
frictionVectors.details: IMF-linked fiscal reforms and major Chinese-financed infrastructure obligations constrain Nairobi's policy autonomy. Debt-service pressures could increase foreign influence over transport and energy assets.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Mombasa remains central to regional trade, exposing Kenya to competition and bargaining pressure from Gulf, Chinese, and neighboring-state interests over logistics infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Highlands Water Project dependence
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's water revenues and infrastructure are tightly linked to South Africa, giving Pretoria substantial leverage over pricing, implementation, and long-term resource governance.

frictionVectors.title: Sovereignty and border vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Economic dependence on South Africa limits Maseru's room to diversify security, trade, and infrastructure partnerships. Periodic political instability compounds this asymmetry.

highlights: Port and logistics access attract strategic competition

frictionVectors.title: Iron ore concession dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large foreign mining operators dominate capital, export logistics, and technical capacity, leaving Liberia exposed to commodity cycles and uneven bargaining power over concessions.

frictionVectors.title: Port and transport infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed control of rail, port, and mining corridors can generate growth but risks concentrating strategic infrastructure outside effective Liberian oversight.

highlights: Oil wealth remains divided by rival authorities
Foreign patrons shape security and export access

frictionVectors.title: Fragmented oil governance
frictionVectors.details: Competing political and armed networks continue to contest control over the National Oil Corporation, export terminals, and budget flows, weakening unified sovereign management.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign military and energy influence
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Russia, Gulf actors, and European states pursue competing security and energy interests in Libya. Their involvement reinforces fragmentation and complicates independent resource policy.

frictionVectors.title: Nickel, cobalt, and mineral concessions
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-controlled mining projects provide export revenue and infrastructure but leave Madagascar exposed to price volatility, tax disputes, and limited domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Mining impact and local consent
frictionVectors.details: Water use, deforestation, and community displacement around major mining operations create recurring tensions over whether resource development serves national or external interests.

frictionVectors.title: External Debt and Policy Conditionality
frictionVectors.details: Malawi remains reliant on IMF support and bilateral creditor restructuring, limiting fiscal autonomy and shaping public-sector reforms.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals and Power Shortages
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed mining investment is expanding, but unreliable electricity and weak transport infrastructure constrain domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Control and Contract Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The military government is pressing foreign gold operators for larger state shares and tighter local control, raising tensions with international firms.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Insecurity and Russian Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian-linked security personnel has displaced Western partners without resolving jihadist violence, while sanctions and regional isolation restrict infrastructure finance.

frictionVectors.title: Energy Corridor Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim gas project strengthens Mauritania's leverage, but dependence on foreign operators, offshore infrastructure, and export markets limits sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Resource Logistics and Local Capture
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, green hydrogen, and port projects attract Gulf, European, and Chinese interest; weak domestic processing capacity leaves substantial value abroad.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos Implementation and Diego Garcia
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius's sovereignty claim has gained diplomatic traction, but the future operating framework for the Diego Garcia base remains sensitive and dependent on major-power agreement.

frictionVectors.title: External Finance and Maritime Exposure
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains diversified and institutionally stable, yet tourism, offshore finance, and imported energy leave it vulnerable to external shocks and regulatory pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Resource Diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: Morocco uses phosphate, fisheries, renewable-energy, and port development in Western Sahara to reinforce its sovereignty claim, sustaining opposition from Algeria and the Polisario Front.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Competition over Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: European, Gulf, Chinese, and U.S. actors compete for roles in ports, renewables, electric vehicles, and logistics, giving Rabat leverage but increasing alignment pressures.

frictionVectors.title: LNG Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The offshore LNG project remains strategically important but depends heavily on foreign operators, international financing, and external security support as insurgent violence persists in Cabo Delgado.

frictionVectors.title: Gas Revenue Governance
frictionVectors.details: Large future gas revenues could strengthen state capacity, but opaque contracting, debt burdens, and weak local participation continue to limit sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Offshore Resources
frictionVectors.details: International energy companies dominate the capital-intensive offshore oil and gas frontier, creating pressure for stronger local-content rules and more favorable fiscal terms.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Port Competition
frictionVectors.details: Walvis Bay and proposed green-hydrogen infrastructure are attracting external investors, raising long-term concerns over strategic assets, export dependence, and control of logistics corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Benin Export Corridor Dispute
frictionVectors.details: Political conflict with Benin has constrained access to the oil-export pipeline, exposing Niger's resource sovereignty to regional transit dependencies and diplomatic pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Alignment
frictionVectors.details: The junta's security partnership with Russia may reduce Western leverage, but reliance on external military support and opaque mining arrangements could replace one dependency with another.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Theft and Pipeline Insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Crude theft, sabotage, and insecurity in the Niger Delta continue to erode state revenue and weaken effective control over strategic energy infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital and Refining Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Domestic refining capacity is expanding, but upstream finance, technology, and trading remain heavily linked to foreign firms and volatile global markets.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern DRC Mineral Flows
frictionVectors.details: International scrutiny remains intense over alleged links between regional armed networks, conflict minerals, and mineral trading routes connected to Rwanda.

frictionVectors.title: External Aid and Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda retains strong administrative control over its domestic economy, but aid, foreign investment, and security partnerships expose its strategic autonomy to diplomatic pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore exploration dependence
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon prospects remain largely speculative, while foreign firms and partners retain the capital and technical leverage over exploration. São Tomé and Príncipe has limited bargaining power if commercially viable reserves emerge.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime security exposure
frictionVectors.details: The archipelago relies on external partners for surveillance and maritime enforcement against illegal fishing and trafficking. Competing interest from Portugal, China, and Gulf actors could constrain strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Gas and oil contract leverage
frictionVectors.details: Production at Sangomar and GTA is strengthening state revenues but leaves Senegal dependent on international operators, lenders, and export infrastructure. Contract transparency and domestic value capture remain central sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Port and logistics competition
frictionVectors.details: Dakar and competing Atlantic corridors attract European, Chinese, Turkish, and Gulf investment. Infrastructure financing can expand capacity while creating long-term strategic and debt dependencies.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign fishing pressure
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles retains strong maritime institutions but remains exposed to distant-water fishing fleets and uneven enforcement capacity. Fisheries access and port services are important sources of leverage for outside powers.

frictionVectors.title: Indian Ocean strategic competition
frictionVectors.details: Indian, Chinese, European, and Gulf actors seek access, influence, and maritime-security cooperation. Victoria must balance infrastructure and security benefits against the risk of becoming overdependent on any external partner.

frictionVectors.title: Iron-ore and mineral concessions
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale mining remains dominated by foreign capital and export logistics, limiting domestic control over pricing, processing, and employment gains. Disputes over taxes, land, and community benefits continue to challenge the state.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor influence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed road, port, and energy projects are essential to connect mines and markets. These arrangements can improve infrastructure while locking public finances and strategic assets into long-term external agreements.

frictionVectors.title: Port and security patronage
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, the Gulf states, the United States, and regional actors provide security and infrastructure support, but their competing interests can fragment national authority. Port access and military cooperation often advance external influence alongside Somali state capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore resource governance
frictionVectors.details: Oil, gas, and fisheries prospects are attracting foreign companies before federal and member-state institutions have fully resolved jurisdiction and revenue-sharing rules. Weak oversight raises the risk of opaque concessions and renewed internal disputes.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral processing dependence
frictionVectors.details: South Africa is seeking greater domestic beneficiation and diversified partnerships for platinum-group metals, manganese, and rare-earth inputs. Foreign investment remains essential, limiting Pretoria's leverage over processing and export terms.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure degradation
frictionVectors.details: Electricity, rail, and port bottlenecks continue to constrain mineral exports and industrial sovereignty. Public-private reforms are advancing, but capital shortages and governance failures leave strategic infrastructure vulnerable.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and export dependence
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan's oil revenue depends on transit infrastructure through Sudan, leaving production and public finances exposed to Sudan's war. Chinese and regional commercial actors retain significant influence over financing, operations, and access.

frictionVectors.title: Elite-controlled resource rents
frictionVectors.details: Political fragmentation and delayed institutional reforms keep oil revenues concentrated among governing elites and security networks. Weak oversight reduces the state's ability to convert resource income into sovereign development capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Gold and militia economies
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and trading networks remain central to financing armed actors, with external buyers and regional intermediaries shaping access and revenue flows. This erodes civilian control over the country's most liquid strategic asset.

frictionVectors.title: Port and energy vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Conflict has damaged transport, refining, and power infrastructure while exposing Port Sudan to strategic competition and military pressure. External support to rival factions further reduces Khartoum's control over national logistics and exports.

frictionVectors.title: LNG bargaining pressure
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is pursuing liquefied natural gas development while negotiating how to retain greater domestic value and fiscal benefit. Major international investors and project-financing requirements constrain the government's room to dictate terms.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Expansion of Dar es Salaam and regional rail links is strengthening Tanzania's position as a logistics hub for landlocked neighbors. Competition among Gulf, Chinese, Indian, and Western investors creates leverage but also raises concerns over long-term concessions.

frictionVectors.title: Port concession dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé remains a major regional gateway and revenue source, but its development depends heavily on foreign logistics, shipping, and finance partners. Concession structures can limit the state's control over strategic trade infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel spillover
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity and instability across the northern frontier are increasing demands on security spending and transport networks. External security cooperation is expanding, creating useful support while complicating strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: European Migration Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: European financial support and migration cooperation give the EU substantial leverage over Tunisian policy. Tunisia seeks funding without accepting an open-ended role as Europe’s migration buffer.

frictionVectors.title: Energy Import Dependence
frictionVectors.details: High dependence on imported gas and electricity constrains strategic autonomy, while delayed renewable-energy investment limits near-term relief.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP Financing and Sanctions
frictionVectors.details: The Uganda-Tanzania oil pipeline remains central to export strategy but faces sustained pressure from environmental groups, Western political scrutiny, and financing constraints. Chinese and Gulf-linked capital remain important to project execution.

frictionVectors.title: Karuma Grid Integration
frictionVectors.details: The Karuma hydropower project improves Uganda’s generation potential but exposes the country to debt-servicing, transmission, and contractor-dependence risks.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-Mineral Competition
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is using competition among Chinese, Western, and Gulf investors to seek better terms in copper and cobalt. Limited domestic processing capacity still leaves substantial value and bargaining power outside the country.

frictionVectors.title: Power Supply Bottleneck
frictionVectors.details: Drought-related hydropower shortages have disrupted mining and industry, increasing dependence on regional electricity imports and emergency generation.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Critical Minerals
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms remain deeply embedded in lithium, platinum, and other mining projects, while Zimbabwe is pressing for local processing without yet possessing sufficient capital or technology to enforce full value addition.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions and Financial Isolation
frictionVectors.details: Western sanctions, restricted access to formal finance, and currency instability increase reliance on informal channels and non-Western partners. This weakens the state’s negotiating position over infrastructure and mineral concessions.
